part_title: Regression Evaluation — MAE, MAPE, RMSE and R-Squared
review_basis: Original AIF Module 03 slides 50–51 visually inspected; diagrams, examples, labels and calculations reviewed against the approved beginner visual-first narration standard.

scenes.title: Model Evaluation – Regression Metrics
scenes.narration: This slide changes the output from a category to a number. Regression predicts quantities, such as a student's test score. On the left, we can see four students represented by hours studied, actual scores, predicted scores and error, defined as actual minus predicted. For two hours, the real score is sixty-five and the prediction is sixty-eight, so the error is minus three. At five hours, seventy-eight minus seventy-five gives plus three. At eight hours, ninety minus eighty-five gives plus five. At ten hours, eighty-eight minus ninety-two gives minus four. Now look at the four metrics on the right. Mean absolute error, or M A E, ignores the plus and minus signs and averages error sizes. Here the absolute errors are three, three, five and four; their total is fifteen, and dividing by four gives three point seven five score points. Mean absolute percentage error, M A P E, divides each absolute error by its actual value and expresses the average as a percentage. This is intuitive but can be unstable or undefined when real values are near zero. Root mean squared error, R M S E, squares the errors before averaging and takes the square root, so larger misses receive stronger penalties. For these example errors the squares are nine, nine, twenty-five and sixteen. The square root of their average, fourteen point seven five, is about three point eight four points. Lastly, R squared compares the model's squared error with the variation around the average actual score. A value close to one can indicate strong explanatory fit on appropriate data, but R squared can be below zero on evaluation data when a model performs worse than predicting the mean. Keep units in mind: M A E and R M S E are in score points; M A P E is a percentage; R squared is a dimensionless comparison. For an application where large mistakes are especially harmful, R M S E may be useful. For an easily interpretable typical miss, M A E is often straightforward.

scenes.title: Regression metrics: choosing the right measurement
scenes.narration: This second illustration repeats the student-score table so we can focus on how to choose a meaningful regression metric. The diagram on the left lists hours studied and actual versus predicted test scores. We are not predicting spam or another class. We are estimating a continuous numerical outcome, and the difference between the estimate and the actual result is the prediction error. Start with M A E at the top of the right side. It describes the typical absolute error in the same units as the output. For the shown four records we found a mean absolute error of three point seven five score points. Next, M A P E describes errors relative to the actual value as a percentage. It might help compare demand forecasts across differently sized items, but beware: an actual value of zero makes the percentage formula undefined, and very small actual values can distort the result. The third row is R M S E, root mean squared error. Because it squares differences before averaging, it pays more attention to a few unusually large misses. The example gives approximately three point eight four points. The final row is R squared. It shows whether a model reduces squared prediction error compared with a simple mean-value baseline. The small rising scatterplot is a visual aid, not a computation of R squared for the displayed students. A large R squared score does not guarantee that every prediction is close, that the model is fair, or that it generalizes beyond this dataset. Always evaluate on representative unseen data and choose metrics relevant to the decision. If an education team needs typical score error in points, which metric is easy to communicate? M A E. If rare very large errors are costly, compare R M S E as well. If actual outcomes can be zero, treat M A P E with caution. This is why there is no universally best metric.
